extracted.intended_audience: communications and public relations (PR) professionals, marketing teams, and anyone writing press releases
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for composing effective press releases that attract media coverage and reader engagement, covering structure, content, length, AP style, SEO, multimedia and distribution considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft a headline with no more than 100 characters that uses strong action verbs to answer the question: “Why should I care?” and prompts your audience to continue reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the headline concise (the page also recommends aiming for 70 characters or less if possible). Capitalize only the first word and proper nouns (AP style). Use strong, unique action verbs (examples: “unveil”, “reveal” often outperform “launch”), write in an active, engaging voice, include numbers or data to back up claims, use relevant keywords, and avoid ambiguous words, vague phrasing and jargon. It should read like an opening to a news story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the city and date showing where and when the press release was issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AP style: Start the first paragraph with the city in all caps, followed by the state abbreviation and the date. Well-known cities may not need the state abbreviation (example: “NEW YORK, May 6, 2024”).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead paragraph (first paragraph / lede)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a summary of the essential details in the first paragraph using the five Ws: who, what, when, where and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with the most crucial information so journalists and readers immediately understand the core news. The lead should answer who, what, when, where and why and set up the rest of the release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body content / supporting paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Expand on the lead paragraph with supporting details and quotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep paragraphs short, focus on one idea per paragraph, and order information so that the most important context comes first. Use quotes and supporting facts to build the story; provide historical context, relevant statistics, survey results or industry trends as supporting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a quote from a relevant stakeholder or expert to add credibility and a human touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quotes to humanize the story and add authority. AP style: use double quotation marks and introduce quotes with the speaker’s full name and title on first reference. Consider quotes from someone directly affected by the news to increase emotional resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide data / credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Back up any claims with relevant statistics, survey results, historical context or industry trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support messages with data from your own research or reputable external sources to build trust and increase the chance of pickup. Cite sources where appropriate and use numbers to substantiate claims in both body copy and headlines when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call to action (CTA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a clear call to action to encourage readers to take the next step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the CTA align with the press release's goal (e.g., link to a microsite or landing page, invite registration for an event, direct readers to more information). Place the CTA where it’s easy for readers and journalists to act on the news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boilerplate
rubrics_metrics.description: Give a brief description of the organization issuing the press release, highlighting its mission and expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the boilerplate short, factual and consistent across releases; include essential context about the organization that helps journalists and readers understand the issuer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide details for media inquiries, including names, emails and phone numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure contact information is up to date and includes the best person for follow-up. Make it easy for reporters to reach someone directly for interviews or fact-checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of images, video and multimedia
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding visual elements can increase engagement with your press release, especially if you add video or images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include high-quality images, videos or other multimedia where appropriate to boost attention and shareability. Provide captions and proper attribution; ensure multimedia is optimized for distribution (file sizes, formats).

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand who your readers are and tailor your message and language accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether you're addressing industry professionals, potential customers or a broader audience. Consider which aspects of the news will resonate most and how the audience prefers to consume information; adjust tone, level of detail and jargon accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be concise
rubrics_metrics.description: All readers appreciate brevity; stick to essential details that support your key information and avoid unnecessary jargon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a press release word count of 300 to 500 words to keep the message clear and focused. Keep paragraphs short and trim anything that doesn't serve the main message. For minor updates, time-sensitive news or teasers, prefer shorter (around 300 words).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay relevant / timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell your audience why they should care and connect the story to timely trends or broader issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link the announcement to current trends, industry developments or social issues when appropriate. A timely and relevant angle increases the likelihood of media pickup and reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell a story / narrative arc
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the press release like a mini-story with a clear beginning, middle and end that weaves a compelling narrative and invites curiosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humanize the story by including anecdotes, quotes from affected people and narrative elements that make the news relatable. Structure the release so the narrative flows logically and builds to the main takeaway.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate SEO
rubrics_metrics.description: Use SEO best practices such as incorporating relevant keywords, optimizing headlines and descriptions and utilizing backlinks to improve discoverability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include keywords naturally in headline and body copy, optimize meta descriptions where possible, and add backlinks to relevant landing pages or resources to boost search engine visibility and referral traffic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review and refine (editing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Edit thoroughly for grammar, style and flow to ensure clarity and accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofread to catch typos and awkward phrasing, then re-read to ensure every word serves a purpose and the key message is clear. Confirm facts, data and names, and polish language for readability before distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length guidance by news type
rubrics_metrics.description: Your exact press release word count will depend on its content; choose shorter or longer formats based on the announcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use shorter ~300-word releases for minor updates, time-sensitive news, or teasers. Use longer releases (over 500 words) when covering complex topics, research/reports, or major announcements like mergers, acquisitions or leadership changes that require more background or technical explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review press release examples / benchmarking
rubrics_metrics.description: It's a good idea to review successful examples of press releases as a starting point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study examples within your industry and for similar purposes (product launches, events, reports) to understand tone, structure and what gets noticed. Use examples as templates but adapt to your unique angle and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: AP Style rules for press releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow Associated Press (AP) Style for journalism and press releases to maintain professional consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key AP-style points from the page: capitalize only the first word and proper nouns in headlines; dateline formatting (city in ALL CAPS, state abbreviation and date); spell out numbers one through nine and use numerals for 10 and above (always use numerals for ages and percentages); date format rules (write month fully when alone/with year; abbreviate certain months when used with dates — Jan., Feb., Aug., Sept., Oct., Nov., Dec.); use double quotation marks for quotes and introduce speakers with full name and title on first reference; capitalize job titles only before a name and lowercase when following a name; spell out an acronym on first use with abbreviation in parentheses and use the abbreviation thereafter; use one space after a period and do not use the Oxford comma; overall structure: put the five Ws in the first paragraph and follow with quotes and supporting information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid jargon and ambiguous phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid unnecessary jargon your audience might not understand and avoid ambiguous or vague phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear, direct language that reads like a news story. Translate technical terms or provide brief explanations when necessary for a broader audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the right distribution partner
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting the right partner (distribution network) affects whether your press release is seen and picked up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use trusted distribution services with broad reach and reporting tools to demonstrate impact; consider geographic and industry targeting to reach relevant media outlets and audiences.
